title: The Sunfish Paradox
excerpt: A fish with a walnut-sized brain has survived 50 million years. Not by being smarter or faster—but by mastering simplicity. The sunfish doesn't try to be a shark. It found its niche and mastered it. With that tiny brain, it can't overthink—it acts on instinct and executes consistently. You don't need to be the smartest in the room. Focus on what sustains you, execute on the basics, and stop measuring yourself against someone else's definition of excellence.
fullText:
The Sunfish Paradox:
What This "Stupid" Fish Teaches Us About Thriving in Business

I came across a YouTube reel about the ocean sunfish the other day, and I haven't been able to stop thinking about it.

By every conventional measure, this creature shouldn't exist. It's slow. It looks awkward. It swims without grace. And here's the kicker: it has one of the smallest brain-to-body ratios of any vertebrate. For a fish that can weigh over 2,000 kg, its brain is roughly the size of a walnut.

Yet it's survived for 50 million years.

1 - We don't need perfection to succeed.
The sunfish isn't trying to be a shark. It's not competing on speed or intelligence. It found its niche and mastered it.

2 - Overthinking kills momentum.
With that tiny brain, the sunfish can't overthink. It acts on instinct, follows simple patterns, and executes consistently.

3 - Scale and presence matter.
The sunfish isn't fast, but its sheer size protects it. In business, this is your brand trust, your network, your market presence.

4 - Build partnerships, not solo empires.
Sunfish survive by letting smaller fish clean them. They know their limits.

5 - Bet on volume, not perfection.
Sunfish produce up to 300 million eggs at once. Most won't make it, but that's the strategy.

6 - Sunfish float and conserve energy.
They understand something we forget: constant motion isn't the same as progress.

You don't need to be the smartest in the room. You just need to focus on what actually sustains you, execute relentlessly on the basics, and stop measuring yourself against someone else's definition of excellence.

title: Patience is Visible
excerpt: The way light falls on an empty chair in a waiting room tells you everything about how the next meeting will go. Patience isn't passive—it's visible. It shows in how we hold space, how we breathe through uncertainty, and how we let moments unfold without forcing them. The best meetings start before anyone speaks.
fullText: The way light falls on an empty chair in a waiting room tells you everything about how the next meeting will go. Patience is visible.

title: The Story Stays
excerpt: For the generations that come after us, it won't be the size of our success that carries forward—it will be the stories we choose to record. I walked into Lucky Bastard Distillers and found their story engraved on every wall, even in the restrooms. Bold, playful, unforgettable. That's when I understood: a life or business can be full of meaning, but its impact lasts only when the story is captured and passed on.
fullText:
For the generations that come after us, it won't be the size of our success that carries forward. What they will remember are the stories we choose to record. A life or a business can be full of meaning, but its impact lasts only when the story is captured and passed on.

That's why the story of Lucky Bastard Distillers stayed with me. Their journey is literally engraved on their walls — even in their restrooms — making sure no one forgets how the distillery was born in Saskatoon.

I actually stumbled into their story by accident. I walked into the men's restroom and saw a big poster of a woman on the wall. For a moment, I thought I had entered the wrong place and stepped back out to check the sign on the door. Later I learned that the poster was part of their storytelling — bold, playful, and unforgettable. That was the moment I understood how deeply they believe in keeping their story alive.

And it's so thoughtful of Jason Aebig, the CEO of the Saskatoon Chamber of Commerce, to choose this venue for the monthly Chamber on Tap. It fits perfectly — a place where the story is part of the experience.

title: Change Can Be Reversed. Evolution Can't.
excerpt: Change is a simple shift from point A to point B. Evolution is a continuous journey where each step aligns with a larger direction. Organizations evolve when their internal changes match the pace of their environment. The Airbus software rollback was still a change—but a reverse one. It restored safety without moving forward. For leaders, the question is simple: Is this change moving us forward, or just moving us?
fullText:
Some conversations change the way ideas move. My chat with Jolene Zidkovich did that for me — the kind where the kinetic energy of ideas suddenly accelerated.

We were talking about something leaders struggle with all the time: the difference between change and evolution.

Change is a simple shift from point A to point B.
Evolution is a continuous journey made of many such shifts, where each step aligns with a larger direction.

In management research, this distinction is clear. Organizations evolve when their internal changes match the pace and direction of their environment — what scholars call "environmental velocity." When a change fits that larger curve, it becomes meaningful and long-term. When it doesn't, it's just movement.

The recent Airbus incident is a real-world example. In late 2025, Airbus discovered that intense solar radiation could corrupt certain flight-control data on A320-family jets. Almost 6,000 aircraft worldwide were asked to undergo a precautionary update. To act quickly, regulators and Airbus rolled back a previous software update until a corrected version is ready.

That rollback is still a change — but it's a reverse change. It restores safety, but it doesn't move the system forward.

And that's the deeper lesson:
Change can be reversed.
Evolution can't.

For leaders, the question is simple:
Is this change moving us forward — or just moving us?

title: Friction Doesn't Hurt the Company. It Hurts the Public.
excerpt: I spent ten minutes in minus 21 trying to pay for parking because the QR code was broken—again. A broken system doesn't reduce the company's revenue. If anything, friction leads to more tickets, and tickets are worth more than fees. So the company doesn't feel the loss. The public does. The management lesson: when you make things easy, people do the right thing. When you build friction, you make money but lose trust.
fullText:
Yesterday I ran into the same problem I faced two months ago. The QR code on this parking stand still hasn't been fixed, and even the app refuses to load the correct location. Nothing has changed.

I was visiting Ashleigh Mattern for a meeting, and before walking in, I spent almost ten minutes in minus 21 trying different ways to pay. Not because the system works well, but because not paying would cost me more in penalties.

And that's the real point here. A broken QR code doesn't reduce the company's revenue. If anything, the friction can lead to more tickets, and a ticket is worth more than a parking fee. So the company doesn't feel the loss. The public does.

The management lesson is simple: when you make things easy, people do the right thing without stress. When you build friction into a system, you might still make money, but you lose trust along the way.

title: Uncertainty Creates Its Own Story
excerpt: A seller on Facebook Marketplace wanted cash 'due to privacy concerns'—even though Interac is one of the safest payment systems in Canada. People don't resist change. They resist uncertainty. When someone is unsure, they fill the gap with assumptions. The real work of change isn't pushing a new system—it's reducing uncertainty through clarity and trust. If we don't explain the change, people will explain it to themselves.
fullText:
I was buying something on Facebook Marketplace this week. Everything looked normal until the seller said he preferred $20 cash "due to privacy concerns."

That line made me pause. In Canada, Interac is one of the safest payment systems we have. It doesn't expose your banking details. It simply shows your name and the email or phone number you choose. There's no real privacy risk.

But this moment reminded me of something deeper that I often see in change management:
People don't resist change. They resist uncertainty.

When someone is unsure, they fill the gap with assumptions. And assumptions create hesitation, even when the new option is clearly safer or more efficient.

In organizations, we see the same pattern. A new process, a new tool, or a new way of working can trigger discomfort—not because it is risky, but because it is unfamiliar. The story we tell ourselves becomes the barrier.

The real work of change is not pushing a new system. It is reducing uncertainty through clarity, trust, and simple communication. When people understand the "why," they stop resisting the "how."

A small Marketplace chat became a reminder:
If we don't explain the change, people will explain it to themselves—and that story is rarely accurate.

title: Winter Weeds
excerpt: I joked with my neighbor: 'If you see any weeds this winter, I'll pluck them.' We laughed—weeds don't grow here in winter. The offer sounded helpful but had no real value. Mobile companies offer extra data we never use. Management creates reports and meetings that look useful but don't move work forward. Real leadership is choosing what matters in the current season—not 'winter weed' tasks.
fullText:
I joked with my neighbor the other day and told him, "If you see any weeds on your lawn this winter, let me know and I'll come pluck them out for you." We both laughed because weeds don't grow here in winter. The offer sounded helpful, but it had no real value.

I see the same thing in everyday life. Mobile companies offer extra gigabytes of data even though many of us never use the full amount we already have. It feels generous, but it doesn't change anything in a practical way.

Management often falls into the same trap. We create reports, meetings, and systems that look useful but don't actually move the work forward. Real leadership is about choosing what matters in the current season and putting energy there, not into "winter weed" tasks.

title: Ethical Responsibility in AI-Driven Platforms
excerpt: I used an AI website builder and received invoices totaling C$1,950 for exceeding quotas—most of it from fixing the AI's own errors. If an AI agent autonomously executes tasks, the platform must own the cost of model hallucination and execution drift. Billing must distinguish between productive work and system-induced retries. AI-powered creation is the future, but the accountability framework must evolve with it—now, not later.
fullText:
I recently used Replit AI website builder for a new project. On the surface, the platform offers a clean value proposition: prompt-driven development, rapid iteration, and a predictable subscription model.

But while building the site, I ran into several problems that point to a deeper issue in how AI execution layers are managed. The model wasn't just making small mistakes. It was displaying clear breakdowns in reasoning — misinterpreting instructions, reversing previously completed steps, creating conflicting layouts, and producing outputs that didn't align with the prompt intent.

When you are trying to complete a task, your attention shifts to stabilizing the system. In those moments, usage quotas and metered-billing alerts, even when they exist, are not meaningful. The urgency becomes correcting the AI's execution drift, not monitoring consumption.

A week later, I received invoices totaling about C$ 1,950 for exceeding the "free quota" attached to the subscription. Most of that usage came from re-running tasks, regenerating pages, and troubleshooting behaviours caused by the model's own inconsistencies.

This raises an important ethical point for AI-driven platforms:

If an AI agent autonomously executes tasks, the platform must take responsibility for the quality of that execution. Customers should not absorb the financial cost of model hallucination, misalignment, execution errors, or system-generated rework.

From an ethical and operational standpoint, three principles feel essential:

1. Execution Accountability — When an AI agent is responsible for generating or modifying work artifacts, the platform should own the cost of errors created by model drift or misalignment.

2. Billing That Reflects Real Conditions — Usage-based billing must distinguish between productive work and system-induced retries. Charging customers for unintended iterations undermines trust.

3. Accessible Human Support — When an AI system triggers unexpected outcomes or billing anomalies, users need a clear path to clarification and resolution.

AI-powered creation is the future, but the accountability framework must evolve with it. The ethics of shifting system inefficiency onto customers is something the entire industry needs to address — not years from now, but now.

title: What Leaders Can Learn from a Pumpkin
excerpt: Pumpkins appear every autumn—bright, grounded, quietly confident. Growth needs space: teams thrive with trust, not control. Nourishment comes from the ground up: stay rooted in empathy and purpose. A tough skin protects a soft core: build boundaries that guard your values. Harvest at the right time: timing matters. Every seed holds another season: nurture people who will grow after you've moved on.
fullText:
What Leaders Can Learn from a Pumpkin

Every autumn, pumpkins appear — bright, grounded, and quietly confident. Beneath their simplicity lie a few timeless lessons for anyone who leads.

1. Growth needs space.
A pumpkin doesn't grow in a pot. It needs open soil and sunlight. Teams are the same — they thrive when given trust and freedom, not control and fear.

2. Nourishment comes from the ground up.
Pumpkins draw strength from the soil. Leaders who stay rooted in empathy, culture, and shared purpose create lasting growth.

3. A tough skin protects a soft core.
The rind isn't harshness — it's protection. Great leaders build healthy boundaries that guard their energy and keep their core values intact.

4. Harvest at the right time.
Pick too early, and it's not ready. Wait too long, and it decays. Timing matters — knowing when to act, pause, or let things ripen makes all the difference.

5. Every seed holds another season.
Inside every pumpkin are hundreds of seeds. Leaders plant ideas and nurture people who will grow long after they've moved on.

Leadership, like a pumpkin, doesn't rush. It just grows — quietly, patiently, and with purpose.

title: Understanding Hysteresis in Change Management
excerpt: Hysteresis comes from physics—a delay before the system catches up. That same pause exists in organizations. You can introduce a new tool or structure, but people don't switch overnight. They hold on to familiar patterns for a while. That lag isn't failure—it's how humans adjust. With AI moving faster than ever, leaders who understand this don't rush. They hold space for transition and give people room to find their footing.
fullText:
We don't often use the word hysteresis in change management.

The word comes from physics, where it means a delay — how some materials don't react right away when forces change. There's always a pause before the system catches up.

That same pause exists in organizations. You can introduce a new tool, structure, or way of working, but people don't switch overnight. They hold on to familiar patterns, fears, and habits for a while. That lag isn't failure — it's part of how humans adjust to new rhythms.

That's what hysteresis looks like in real life — the quiet space between change and acceptance.

Now, with AI moving faster than ever, that space feels even more visible. Technology races ahead, but people still need time to learn, trust, and adapt. Hysteresis reminds us that real progress isn't about keeping pace with machines — it's about helping people stay steady as the world speeds up.

Leaders who understand this don't rush the process. They hold space for transition and give people room to find their footing. Because change isn't about how fast we move forward — it's about how well we bring everyone along.
